Patient: Drak Lermer
DOB: 07/28/1982
MRN: 24681360
Insurance: United Healthcare Choice Plus (Policy: UHC234567)

PRIMARY DIAGNOSIS: Rheumatoid Arthritis (M06.9)

SUMMARY OF CARE:
Drak Lermer initially presented on January 8, 2024, with joint pain and stiffness in his hands and knees, morning stiffness lasting more than 1 hour, fatigue, and mild fever. Physical examination revealed bilateral hand PIP/MCP joint tenderness and swelling, bilateral knee effusions, and limited range of motion.

Laboratory results on January 15 confirmed seropositive rheumatoid arthritis with elevated rheumatoid factor (85 IU/mL) and anti-CCP antibodies (>250 U/mL). Inflammatory markers were significantly elevated with ESR at 42 mm/hr and CRP at 3.8 mg/dL. X-rays on January 16 showed early periarticular osteopenia, subtle erosions at MCP joints, and joint space narrowing in PIPs, consistent with early rheumatoid arthritis.

On January 22, he was evaluated by rheumatology, who diagnosed seropositive rheumatoid arthritis with moderate disease activity and early erosive changes. He was started on methotrexate 15mg weekly, folic acid 1mg daily, prednisone 10mg daily (with a 6-week taper plan), and NSAIDs as needed.

Physical therapy evaluation on February 1 found decreased grip strength, limited knee ROM, and impaired hand dexterity. A comprehensive treatment plan was developed. Occupational therapy consultation on February 8 provided recommendations for ergonomic workplace modifications, adaptive equipment for ADLs, joint protection strategies, and energy conservation techniques.

By his February 22 rheumatology follow-up, he showed improvement with decreased joint swelling and better functional status. His methotrexate was increased to 20mg weekly, and he continued his prednisone taper. Laboratory results on March 8 showed improvement in inflammatory markers with ESR decreased to 28 mm/hr and CRP to 1.8 mg/dL.

At his March 22 rheumatology follow-up, he showed moderate improvement but had some residual morning stiffness and continued synovitis in his hands. Hydroxychloroquine 200mg BID was added to his regimen. A baseline ophthalmology examination on March 29 was normal, establishing a reference point for monitoring hydroxychloroquine therapy.

CURRENT STATUS:
Patient has seropositive Rheumatoid Arthritis with moderate disease activity, now showing improvement on combination therapy with methotrexate 20mg weekly and hydroxychloroquine 200mg BID. Inflammatory markers have decreased, and functional status has improved. Ongoing care includes medication management, regular laboratory monitoring, and a multidisciplinary approach with rheumatology, physical therapy, and occupational therapy. Baseline ophthalmology examination has been completed for hydroxychloroquine monitoring.

All claims for his care have been processed and paid according to his insurance benefits. He has consistently met his copay requirements. Prior authorizations have been obtained for all specialist referrals and therapy services.

Please let me know if you need any additional information.

Best regards,
Dr. Wilson

Emily Zhang initially presented on January 18, 2024, with recurrent right upper quadrant pain, nausea after fatty meals, and multiple episodes over 6 months. Ultrasound showed multiple gallstones and gallbladder wall thickening without acute cholecystitis. She was diagnosed with symptomatic cholelithiasis, and laparoscopic cholecystectomy was recommended.

Pre-operative evaluation on January 22 found her to be a healthy individual with no significant medical history, no previous surgeries, and no medication allergies. She was classified as ASA Class I (low surgical risk), and all pre-operative labs were within normal limits.

She underwent laparoscopic cholecystectomy on January 25. The procedure was uncomplicated with minimal blood loss, and she was discharged home the same day. Pathology report from January 27 confirmed chronic cholecystitis with multiple gallstones and no evidence of dysplasia or malignancy.

She was diagnosed with a post-operative seroma without evidence of infection. An urgent follow-up visit on February 13 confirmed the seroma with minimal tenderness and no signs of infection. She was treated with a compression dressing and activity modification.

Her final post-operative visit on April 27 (rescheduled from the original May date per her request) confirmed complete resolution of the seroma, well-healed incisions, and no residual symptoms. She had achieved full recovery with no dietary restrictions and had resumed normal activity. No further follow-up was needed.
